topics.title: Add a scalar to every element
topics.body: A scalar is broadcast across the whole array, so one `+` replaces a loop. No Python-level iteration happens.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Compare an array with a scalar
topics.body: Comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape. That array is what every filter is built on.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 5, 9]) > 4)

topics.title: A Python loop still works over an array
topics.body: Iterating walks the first axis. It is fine for a handful of values and wrong for a million, where a vectorised expression wins.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

total = 0
for value in np.array([2, 4, 6]):
    total += int(value)
print(total)

topics.title: Every array reports its own type
topics.body: `np.array` always returns an `ndarray`. A Python `list` and an `ndarray` are not interchangeable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(type(np.array([1, 2])).__name__)

topics.title: ndim counts the axes
topics.body: `ndim` is how many indices you need to reach a single value; `size` is how many values exist in total.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.zeros((2, 3, 4))
print(a.ndim, a.size)

topics.title: Ten zeros are one dimension
topics.body: A one-dimensional array has a trailing comma in its shape. That is a 1-tuple, not a scalar.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.zeros(10).shape)

topics.title: Shape is a tuple you can index
topics.body: `shape` is data, not a method. Read `shape[0]` for rows and `shape[1]` for columns instead of calling it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 2))
print(a.shape[0], a.shape[1])

topics.title: A matrix of one row still has two axes
topics.body: Wrapping a list in a list adds an axis even when there is only one element in it. Shape `(1, 2)` is a matrix, `(2,)` is a vector.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[7, 8]]).shape)

topics.title: empty allocates without setting values
topics.body: `np.empty` skips initialisation, so it is faster but holds whatever memory was there. Use it only when you overwrite every element next.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.empty(3)
print(a.shape, a.dtype)

topics.title: identity builds an identity matrix
topics.body: `np.identity(n)` is the square identity: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.identity(2))

topics.title: arange counts down with a negative step
topics.body: The stop value is excluded in both directions. A negative step reverses the walk through the range.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(5, 0, -1))

topics.title: linspace controls the step you get
topics.body: `linspace(start, stop, n)` includes the endpoint and spaces `n` values evenly, which `arange` with floats cannot promise.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))

topics.title: dtype reports the element type
topics.body: The dtype belongs to the whole array, not to each element. Mixing an int and a float array promotes to float.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0]).dtype)

topics.title: A float array prints a decimal point
topics.body: The printed form already tells you the dtype: `[1. 2.]` is float, `[1 2]` is int. Reading the output is faster than checking.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2], dtype=float))

topics.title: Each dtype has a size in bytes
topics.body: `itemsize` is bytes per element. Ten million `int64` values need 80 MB before any copy, which is why dtype choice is a memory decision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dtype('int64').itemsize, np.dtype('int32').itemsize)

topics.title: A comparison produces booleans
topics.body: Masks are a dtype, not a special object. `bool` arrays are one byte per element and are the currency of filtering.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([1, 2, 3]) > 1).dtype)

topics.title: Negative indices count from the end
topics.body: `-1` is the last element, `-2` the one before it. The same rule applies to slices and to every axis.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[-1], a[-2])

topics.title: Slice columns of a matrix
topics.body: The colon means "every row", the number picks one column. The result loses that axis and becomes one-dimensional.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 1])

topics.title: A boolean mask filters one dimension
topics.body: The mask must match the array's shape. Elements where the mask is `True` are copied into a new, shorter array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([5, 6, 7])
print(a[a > 5])

topics.title: Index with paired row and column lists
topics.body: Two index arrays are zipped, not crossed: element `i` of the result comes from row `rows[i]`, column `cols[i]`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[[0, 2], [1, 2]])

topics.title: The end of a slice is exclusive
topics.body: `a[2:5]` keeps positions 2, 3 and 4. Off-by-one bugs in NumPy almost always come from forgetting this.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:5])

topics.title: Omit a bound to keep it open
topics.body: `a[:2]` starts at zero, `a[3:]` runs to the end. Leaving a bound out is the idiomatic way to say "from the edge".
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print(a[:2], a[3:])

topics.title: A step of two skips elements
topics.body: The third slot of a slice is the step. It can be larger than one or negative, and it never changes the source array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(10)[::2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns at once
topics.body: Each axis gets its own slice separated by a comma. The result is a rectangular block, never a ragged one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[1:, :2])

topics.title: ravel flattens without copying when it can
topics.body: A contiguous array can be flattened as a view. `base` proves whether the new array still points at the old memory.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.ravel().base is a)

topics.title: reshape turns a vector into a column
topics.body: `(4, 1)` and `(1, 4)` look similar but broadcast in opposite directions. The shape is the whole difference.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
print(a.reshape(4, 1))

topics.title: vstack stacks arrays into rows
topics.body: `vstack` adds a new first axis, so two `(2,)` arrays become one `(2, 2)` array. `hstack` joins along the existing axis instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.vstack([np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4])]))

topics.title: Transpose swaps the axes
topics.body: `.T` reverses the axis order and is a view, not a copy. For a matrix it swaps rows with columns.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.shape)

topics.title: Exponentiation uses the ** operator
topics.body: `**` is elementwise on arrays. `np.power` is the same operation written as a function when you need it as a callback.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 3]) ** 2)

topics.title: abs works on whole arrays
topics.body: NumPy's functions accept arrays, lists and scalars through the same call. That consistency is what makes them composable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.abs(np.array([-3, 4])))

topics.title: cumsum keeps every running total
topics.body: `cumsum` returns an array of the same length, while `sum` collapses it to one number. Use the cumulative form for running balances and charts.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.cumsum(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

topics.title: log and exp invert each other
topics.body: Applying `exp` after `log` returns the original numbers up to floating-point error, which is exactly what `allclose` is for.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1.0, 10.0])
print(np.allclose(np.exp(np.log(values)), values))

topics.title: A row array broadcasts across rows
topics.body: A `(3,)` array lines up with the last axis of a `(2, 3)` array. That is the rule that makes row-wise maths a single line.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a + np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)

topics.title: A scalar is the smallest broadcast
topics.body: Scalars stretch to every position without copying. The result is a new array of the original shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())

topics.title: Broadcast a column against a row
topics.body: A `(2, 1)` column and a `(2,)` row produce a `(2, 2)` grid — every combination, with no explicit loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([[1], [2]]) * np.array([10, 20])).tolist())

topics.title: A size of one stretches automatically
topics.body: An axis of length 1 is repeated to match the other operand. That is why `(3, 1) + ones(4)` becomes `(3, 4)`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.zeros((3, 1)) + np.ones(4)).shape)

topics.title: mean of a matrix returns one number
topics.body: Without `axis`, a reduction flattens the array first. The result is a scalar, not a one-element array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).mean())

topics.title: axis=1 reduces each row
topics.body: The reduced axis disappears. Row sums are therefore one value per row, in a `(2,)` array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]).sum(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: std measures spread in the same units
topics.body: Variance is squared units; the standard deviation puts it back in the original scale, which is why reports use it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]).std())

topics.title: The maximum and where it lives
topics.body: `max` gives the value, `argmax` gives its position. Both accept an `axis` when you need one answer per row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([3, 9, 4])
print(a.max(), a.argmax())

topics.title: A mask keeps the shape of its array
topics.body: Comparing an array to a number never shortens it. Only indexing with the mask does that.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print((a % 2 == 0).shape)

topics.title: where chooses between two values
topics.body: `np.where(mask, a, b)` is a vectorised `if`. Neither branch is skipped, so both should be cheap expressions.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.where(np.array([1, 5, 2]) > 3, 'big', 'small').tolist())

topics.title: Sum the mask to count matches
topics.body: `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0, so `sum` on a mask is a count. Wrap it in `int` when you want a Python number.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(int((np.arange(10) > 5).sum()))

topics.title: Filter a matrix elementwise
topics.body: Indexing with a full-shape mask flattens the matches into a 1-D array. Row structure is not preserved.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[a % 2 == 0].tolist())

topics.title: argsort returns the order, not the values
topics.body: The output holds positions, so it is the right tool for sorting one array by another. Feed it to the data to reorder.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.argsort(np.array([3, 1, 2])).tolist())

topics.title: sort can work in place
topics.body: `ndarray.sort()` rearranges the array itself and returns `None`. `np.sort` returns a new array instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[3, 1], [2, 4]])
a.sort(axis=1)
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: unique removes repeats and sorts
topics.body: The result is always sorted, even if the input was not. Add `return_counts=True` to see how often each value appeared.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.unique(np.array([3, 1, 3, 2])).tolist())

topics.title: argmin finds the smallest position
topics.body: It returns the first occurrence on ties, which makes it safe for lookups where duplicates are possible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.argmin(np.array([4, 2, 8])))

topics.title: A slice is a view into the source
topics.body: Assigning into the slice writes into the original buffer. Nothing was copied when the slice was taken.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
b = a[:2]
b[0] = 99
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: A copy stops the sharing
topics.body: `.copy()` allocates a new buffer, so writes to it never reach the source. This is the fix for accidental mutation.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
b = a[:2].copy()
b[0] = 99
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Strides describe how memory is walked
topics.body: The stride is bytes to step per axis. A transposed or sliced array needs no new memory because only the strides change.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3).strides)

topics.title: A reshape can stay a view
topics.body: If the layout allows it, `reshape` returns a view whose `base` is the original array. A transpose or a non-contiguous slice forces a copy.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
print(b.base is a)

topics.title: integers excludes the high value
topics.body: `rng.integers(low, high)` is half-open, like `range`. Asking for `(0, 2)` can only yield 0 or 1.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.integers(0, 2, size=5).max() <= 1)

topics.title: The seed decides the whole stream
topics.body: Two generators made with the same seed produce identical draws. That is how a random example becomes reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

first = np.random.default_rng(42).random(3).round(3).tolist()
second = np.random.default_rng(42).random(3).round(3).tolist()
print(first == second)

topics.title: choice samples without replacement
topics.body: `replace=False` behaves like drawing cards: no value repeats. With `replace=True` a value can appear several times.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
draw = rng.choice(5, 3, replace=False)
print(len(set(draw.tolist())) == 3)

topics.title: normal draws cluster around the mean
topics.body: The mean of many standard normal draws approaches zero. Increasing the sample size tightens the estimate, not the spread.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
sample = rng.normal(0, 1, 10000)
print(abs(sample.mean()) < 0.05)

topics.title: identity is the matrix version of one
topics.body: Multiplying by `np.identity(n)` leaves a matrix unchanged. It is the natural sanity check for a matmul pipeline.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0]])
print(np.allclose(A @ np.identity(2), A))

topics.title: Transpose flips a matrix product
topics.body: `(A @ B).T` equals `B.T @ A.T`. The order swaps, which is the property behind many derivations.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
B = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]])
print(np.allclose((A @ B).T, B.T @ A.T))

topics.title: A zero determinant means no unique solution
topics.body: A singular matrix has linearly dependent rows, so `solve` cannot return one answer. Check the determinant before trusting a fit.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(round(float(np.linalg.det(np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 4.0]]))), 6))

topics.title: trace sums the diagonal
topics.body: The trace needs no square-matrix maths beyond the diagonal. It equals the sum of the eigenvalues.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.trace(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])))

topics.title: Save one array and load it back
topics.body: `np.save` writes a binary `.npy` file and `np.load` restores the values and dtype exactly, with no parsing.
topics.code:
import os
import tempfile
import numpy as np

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_roundtrip.npy')
np.save(path, np.array([1, 2, 3]))
print(np.load(path))

topics.title: genfromtxt reads named columns
topics.body: `names=True` treats the first row as field names, turning a CSV into a structured array you index by name.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
from io import StringIO

text = 'a,b\n1,2\n3,4'
data = np.genfromtxt(StringIO(text), delimiter=',', names=True)
print(data['a'].tolist())

topics.title: loadtxt skips comment lines
topics.body: Lines starting with `#` are ignored by default. Passing `dtype=int` keeps the numbers as integers instead of floats.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
from io import StringIO

print(np.loadtxt(StringIO('# n\n1\n2\n'), dtype=int))

topics.title: An npz file exposes its arrays by key
topics.body: `np.savez` stores several named arrays in one archive. `np.load` returns a mapping-like object that lists those names.
topics.code:
import os
import tempfile
import numpy as np

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_keys.npz')
np.savez(path, a=np.arange(2), b=np.arange(3))
print(sorted(np.load(path)))

topics.title: char functions work elementwise on text
topics.body: The `np.char` namespace applies string methods to every element without a Python loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.char.upper(np.array(['np', 'ai'])).tolist())

topics.title: str_len counts characters
topics.body: Length is a property of the string, not the fixed-width buffer. Padding does not inflate the count.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.char.str_len(np.array(['ab', 'cde'])).tolist())

topics.title: Datetime differences are timedeltas
topics.body: Subtracting two `datetime64` values gives a `timedelta64`, which converts to a number by dividing by a unit.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

start = np.datetime64('2026-01-01')
end = np.datetime64('2026-01-11')
print((end - start) / np.timedelta64(1, 'D'))

topics.title: A structured array reads fields by name
topics.body: One row can hold several dtypes. Field access returns a normal array, so all the usual reductions apply.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

dtype = np.dtype([('name', 'U4'), ('score', 'i4')])
rows = np.array([('ada', 91)], dtype=dtype)
print(rows['score'].tolist())

topics.title: NaN never equals itself
topics.body: IEEE 754 defines `NaN != NaN`, so equality checks can never find missing values. Use `np.isnan` instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.nan == np.nan)

topics.title: isnan finds missing values
topics.body: The result is a boolean array, ready to be inverted with `~` or counted with `sum`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.isnan(np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])).tolist())

topics.title: nanstd ignores the gaps
topics.body: The `nan`-prefixed reductions skip missing values. Plain `std` would return `nan` for the whole array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(round(float(np.nanstd(np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0]))), 6))

topics.title: Mask NaN, then reduce
topics.body: Filtering with `~np.isnan(a)` is the explicit alternative to the `nan`-prefixed functions and works with any reduction.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(a[~np.isnan(a)].mean())

topics.title: add.reduce sums along an axis
topics.body: Every ufunc has a `reduce` that applies it down an axis. It is the general form behind `sum`, `prod` and `max`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.add.reduce(np.arange(5)))

topics.title: einsum can read a diagonal
topics.body: Repeating an index in `einsum` means "same position on both axes", which extracts or sums the diagonal without a mask.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(np.einsum('ii->', A))

topics.title: bincount needs non-negative integers
topics.body: The output length is one more than the largest value, so position `i` counts how often `i` appeared. Floats raise a `TypeError`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])).tolist())

topics.title: dot on matrices is a matrix product
topics.body: On two 2-D arrays, `np.dot` and `@` agree. Confusing it with elementwise `*` is the classic shape bug.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dot(np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]]), np.array([2, 3])).tolist())

topics.title: Scale each row by its own maximum
topics.body: `keepdims=True` keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the division broadcasts back across the row without reshaping.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 6.0]])
print((a / a.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)).round(3).tolist())

topics.title: diff gives step-to-step change
topics.body: `np.diff` returns one fewer value than the input: the difference between each neighbouring pair.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.diff(np.array([100.0, 110.0, 99.0])).round(3).tolist())

topics.title: digitize buckets values into bins
topics.body: The output is the index of the bin each value falls into. By default the right edge is open, so `0.5` lands in the next bucket.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.digitize(np.array([0.1, 0.5, 1.5]), [0.5, 1.0]).tolist())

topics.title: Build a confusion matrix with bincount
topics.body: Encoding a pair of labels as `true * classes + predicted` turns the counts into a matrix with one reshape and no loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

truth = np.array([1, 0, 1])
predicted = np.array([1, 1, 1])
counts = np.bincount(truth * 2 + predicted, minlength=4)
print(counts.reshape(2, 2).tolist())
